newsitem.title: USA: Flaws found in U.S. Senate election, chairman says.
newsitem.headline: Flaws found in U.S. Senate election, chairman says.

text.p: Democrats are willing to discuss the disputed U.S. Senate election in Louisiana but it will not change the fact that Mary Landrieu won, Democratic Senator Wendell Ford said Friday.

Earlier this week, Democrats said they would no longer take part in an investigation ordered by the Republican majority on the Senate Rules Committee. Their refusal put the future of the investigation in doubt.

Rules chairman John Warner, Virginia Republican, said he would try to arrange a committee meeting after the Independence Day recess to try to iron out the dispute. He said the review ought to continue.
"Democrats on the Rules Committee are not opposed to a hearing on this investigation," responded Ford, of Kentucky, his party's leader on the panel.
"I just hope my colleagues on the other side come prepared to hear the truth -- the truth that this investigation is completed."
The Republican candidate, Louis "Woody" Jenkins, has contended that vote fraud allowed Landrieu, a Democrat, to claim victory by 5,788 votes out of 1.7 million cast.
Landrieu was sworn into office Jan. 7, pending the outcome of an investigation into Jenkins' complaints.
Ford said the investigation was over budget and behind schedule and found nothing to question Landrieu's victory.

Warner said while investigators have found few of the "phantom votes" alleged by Jenkins, they have found that fair-election safeguards "were breached, broken, in many instances." In some cases, records were not sealed and voting machines were opened without witnesses present.
The possibility of fraud that affected the election merited investigation, he said.
